subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Welcome back to Ehel Academy Science. You are now in Year 8, and you already know a great deal about how living things are built and how they stay alive. This year we turn to one of the deepest questions in all of biology: how does life continue from one generation to the next? Every living thing eventually grows old and dies, yet life on Earth never runs out. The secret is reproduction — the way living things make new individuals like themselves. In this unit you will discover how plants, the quiet green organisms all around you, carry out this remarkable task.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Describe how science is applied across societies and industries, and in research.
Plan a range of investigations of different types, while considering variables appropriately, and recognise that not all investigations can be fair tests.
Identify different ecosystems on the Earth, recognising the variety of habitats that exist within an ecosystem.
Describe the impact of the bioaccumulation of toxic substances on an ecosystem.
Describe how a new and/or invasive species can affect other organisms and an ecosystem.

outcomes: Explain the difference between asexual and sexual reproduction in plants, and give examples of each.
Describe several methods of asexual reproduction in plants, including runners, bulbs, tubers, and how farmers use cuttings and grafting.
Name and label the main parts of an insect-pollinated flower and state the job of each part.
Explain the difference between the male parts (stamen) and the female parts (carpel) of a flower.
Describe pollination and distinguish between insect pollination and wind pollination.
Explain fertilisation in a flowering plant and what happens after it.
Describe how seeds and fruits form from a fertilised flower.
Explain why seed dispersal matters and describe the main methods plants use to spread their seeds.
Describe the conditions needed for germination and outline the life cycle of a flowering plant.
Explain how farmers use their knowledge of plant reproduction to grow better crops.

concepts.title: Two Ways to Make New Plants
concepts.explanation:
Plants make new plants in two very different ways, and a great many plants can use both. Understanding the difference between these two ways is the foundation for everything else in this unit, so let us build it carefully.

The first way is asexual reproduction. In asexual reproduction there is only one parent, and no sex cells join together. Instead, part of the parent plant simply grows into a new, complete plant. Because the new plant is made from the cells of a single parent, it is an exact copy — a clone — of that parent. It has the same instructions, the same DNA, and so it looks the same, tastes the same, and behaves the same. When a banana plant sends up a young shoot beside itself, that shoot is a clone of the parent banana. When a farmer plants a piece of stem from a sweet cassava plant and it grows roots, the new cassava is genetically identical to the one it came from.

The second way is sexual reproduction. Here there are two parents, and a male sex cell joins a female sex cell to make the first cell of a brand-new individual. The joining of these two cells is called fertilisation. Because the new plant receives instructions from two parents mixed together, it is not identical to either one. It is a little different from both, just as brothers and sisters in a family resemble their parents but are not exactly like either of them. Most flowering plants reproduce sexually using their flowers, which is why so much of this unit is about how flowers work.

Why do plants have two methods? Each has its own advantages, and this is a beautiful example of design that suits the needs of the living thing. Asexual reproduction is fast and reliable. A single healthy parent can make many identical offspring without needing another plant nearby, and every offspring will carry the good qualities of the parent. This is exactly why farmers love it: if you find one mango tree that gives especially sweet fruit, you can copy it again and again by taking cuttings or by grafting, and every new tree will give the same sweet fruit. But there is a weakness. Because the clones are all identical, if a disease or a drought can harm one of them, it can harm them all. There is no variety to fall back on.

Sexual reproduction is slower and needs pollen to be carried from one flower to another, but it has a priceless advantage: it produces variation. The offspring are all a little different from one another. In a changing world — where a new plant disease might arrive, or the rains might fail, or the soil might change — this variety means that some of the offspring may be better suited to survive. Variation is the raw material that allows living things to adapt over many generations. So the two methods together give plants both reliability and the ability to change. Keep this comparison in your mind; we will return to it at the end of the unit.
concepts.example: 🌟 Did You Know? The oldest date palms of the north are often grown from offshoots — small shoots that appear at the base of the parent palm. A prized variety of sweet date can be kept exactly the same for hundreds of years by planting these offshoots, so the dates a family eats today may taste identical to those their great-great-grandparents enjoyed.

concepts.title: Asexual Reproduction in Plants
concepts.explanation:
Let us look more closely at the clever ways plants make copies of themselves without seeds. Nature invented asexual reproduction long before farmers ever used it, and once you know what to look for, you will see it happening in gardens and fields all around you.

Some plants grow a long, thin stem that creeps sideways along the surface of the soil. This creeping stem is called a runner or a stolon. Every so often the runner touches the ground, grows little roots, and a new plant springs up. The grasses of the savanna spread across the land in exactly this way, which is why grass can cover a whole field so quickly after the rains. A strawberry plant, if you have ever seen one, sends out runners in the same manner. The new plants are clones of the parent, joined to it by the runner until they are strong enough to live on their own.

A bulb is a short underground stem packed with fleshy leaves full of stored food, rather like a natural food store buried in the soil. The onions in your kitchen are bulbs. A single bulb can grow small side bulbs beside itself, and each of these can grow into a new plant next season. Garlic works the same way: each clove you plant grows into a whole new bulb. The stored food gives the young plant a strong, quick start, which is a great advantage in a place where the growing season is short.

A tuber is a swollen underground part of a plant, filled with stored food, that can grow into new plants. The potato is the most famous example: each potato has several small 'eyes', and every eye can sprout into a new potato plant. Sweet potatoes and yams, grown in many parts of East Africa, spread in a similar way. Farmers simply plant pieces of the tuber, each with an eye, and new plants grow from them — no seeds required.

How Farmers Use Asexual Reproduction: Cuttings

For thousands of years farmers have used asexual reproduction on purpose to grow the plants they want. The simplest method is taking a cutting. A cutting is a piece of stem cut from a healthy parent plant. When the cut end is pushed into moist soil, it grows new roots and becomes a complete new plant, identical to its parent. Cassava is very commonly grown from stem cuttings across East Africa: a farmer near the Shabelle River can cut a mature cassava stem into short lengths, push them into the ground at the start of the rains, and grow a whole new field. Banana plants, sugar cane, and many garden shrubs are grown this way too. Because the new plant is a clone, the farmer knows exactly what he will get.

How Farmers Use Asexual Reproduction: Grafting

A cleverer method, and one especially important for fruit trees like mango and citrus, is grafting. In grafting, a farmer joins a shoot or bud from one plant, called the scion, onto the root and lower stem of another plant, called the rootstock. The two are bound tightly together, and as they heal they join and grow as one plant. The farmer chooses a scion from a tree that gives excellent sweet fruit, and a rootstock that has strong roots and resists disease and drought. The result is a single tree with the best of both: sweet fruit above and tough roots below. This is how the many identical sweet-mango trees in an orchard near Afgooye are produced. Every grafted mango tree carries fruit exactly like the parent tree the scion came from, which would be impossible if the trees were grown from seed, because seeds produce variation.
concepts.example: Notice the pattern in all of these methods: one parent, no sex cells joining, and offspring that are exact copies. That is the signature of asexual reproduction. Now we turn to the other great method, the one that happens inside a flower.

concepts.title: The Flower — An Organ Built for Reproduction
concepts.explanation:
A flower may look to us like a pretty decoration, but to the plant it is a serious and important organ: it is the structure built entirely for sexual reproduction. Every part of a flower has a job to do in making seeds. Let us take a typical insect-pollinated flower, such as a hibiscus or a bean flower, and tour its parts from the outside in. Picture the flower in your mind as we go, and try to draw it afterwards.

On the very outside of the flower, at the base, are the sepals. Before the flower opens, the sepals form a green protective covering around the bud, shielding the delicate parts inside as they develop. Once the flower opens, you can still see the sepals as small green leaf-like flaps beneath the petals.

Just inside the sepals are the petals. In insect-pollinated flowers the petals are usually large, brightly coloured, and sometimes scented. Their job is to attract insects such as bees and butterflies. Deep inside many flowers, at the base of the petals, are small glands called nectaries that make a sweet liquid called nectar. Insects come to drink the nectar, and while they are busy feeding, they brush against the flower's reproductive parts and carry pollen away with them. The bright colour is like a signboard over a shop, and the nectar is the reward that keeps the insect visitors coming.

Inside the ring of petals we reach the reproductive parts. The male part of the flower is the stamen, and a flower usually has several of them. Each stamen has two parts. At the top is the anther, a small bag that makes and holds the pollen grains. Pollen is a fine dust, often yellow, and each tiny grain carries a male sex cell (male gamete). Holding the anther up on a thin stalk is the filament. So when you see fine yellow dust on your fingers after touching a flower, you have touched pollen from the anthers of its stamens.

At the very centre of the flower is the female part, called the carpel (sometimes called the pistil). It is shaped rather like a flask, and it has three parts. At the top is the stigma, a sticky surface whose job is to catch pollen grains that land on it. Below the stigma is a stalk called the style, which connects the stigma to the base. At the base, swollen and rounded, is the ovary. Inside the ovary are one or more ovules, and each ovule contains a female sex cell, the egg cell (female gamete). After fertilisation, each ovule will become a seed, and the ovary itself will become the fruit.

🌟 Did You Know? A single sunflower head is not one flower but hundreds of tiny flowers packed together, and each one can make a seed. That is why one sunflower head gives you a whole handful of seeds. Nature often hides many flowers inside what looks like one.
concepts.example: Here is a helpful way to remember the two reproductive parts. The stamen is the male part; think of the words 'stamen' and 'man'. It is made of anther and filament. The carpel is the female part; it is made of stigma, style, and ovary, and it holds the ovules that will become seeds. Everything else — sepals, petals, nectar — exists to protect these parts and to help pollen travel from the male part of one flower to the female part of another.

concepts.title: Pollination — Delivering the Pollen
concepts.explanation:
For sexual reproduction to happen, the male sex cell inside a pollen grain must reach the female egg cell inside an ovule. But pollen is made up in the anther, and the egg is hidden away in the ovary at the base of the carpel. The first step of the journey is to move pollen from an anther onto a stigma. This transfer of pollen from anther to stigma is called pollination. Be careful here: pollination is only the delivery of the pollen. It is not the same as fertilisation, which comes later. Many students confuse these two, so hold the difference firmly: pollination is the journey of the pollen; fertilisation is the joining of the sex cells.

There are two kinds of pollination worth knowing. Self-pollination happens when pollen lands on the stigma of the same flower, or another flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination happens when pollen is carried to the flower of a different plant of the same kind. Cross-pollination mixes the instructions of two separate plants and so produces more variation, which is usually healthier for the species. Plants use two main helpers to carry pollen from flower to flower: insects and the wind.

Many flowers are pollinated by insects, especially bees. These insect-pollinated flowers are built to attract and use their insect visitors. They have large, brightly coloured, scented petals and sweet nectar to draw insects in. Their anthers are held firmly inside the flower so that a visiting insect must brush past them, picking up sticky pollen on its body. Their stigmas are also inside the flower and are sticky, so that pollen rubs off onto them from the next insect that visits. When a bee flies from a mango blossom near Afgooye to another mango tree, the pollen caught in the hairs of its body is carried along and rubbed onto the new flower's stigma. In this way the bee, seeking only food, becomes the plant's delivery service. Mango, papaya, beans, sunflower, and most fruit trees are pollinated by insects.

Other flowers are pollinated by the wind. These wind-pollinated flowers look completely different, and once you know why, the differences make perfect sense. Because they do not need to attract insects, they have small, dull petals or none at all, and they make no nectar and little scent — there would be no point wasting energy on them. Instead they make huge amounts of light, smooth pollen that blows easily on the breeze. Their anthers hang outside the flower, dangling in the wind so that the pollen is easily carried away. Their stigmas are large and feathery and also hang outside, spread out like a net to catch pollen drifting through the air. Maize and sorghum, the great grain crops grown along the Jubba and Shabelle rivers, are wind-pollinated, and so are all the grasses of the savanna. If you have ever walked through a field of maize and seen a cloud of yellow dust rise when the plants are shaken, you have watched wind pollination happening before your eyes.

concepts.title: Fertilisation — The Sex Cells Join
concepts.explanation:
Pollination has delivered a pollen grain onto the stigma. Now the real meeting must take place, deep inside the flower. This is fertilisation: the joining of the male sex cell from the pollen with the female egg cell inside the ovule. Let us follow the journey step by step, because it is one of the most elegant processes in nature.

A pollen grain lands on the sticky stigma and sticks there.

The pollen grain grows a fine tube, called a pollen tube, which pushes down through the style toward the ovary. It is as if the pollen grain grows a tiny root that tunnels down inside the flower.

The pollen tube grows all the way down until it reaches an ovule inside the ovary.

The male sex cell (the nucleus from the pollen) travels down the tube and joins with the female egg cell inside the ovule. This joining of the two sex cells is fertilisation.

The fertilised egg cell is now the first cell of a new plant. It will grow into a tiny young plant called an embryo.

Fertilisation is the true beginning of a new plant. Before it, we had only two separate half-instructions: the male sex cell and the female egg cell. After it, we have one complete cell carrying instructions from two parents, ready to grow into a whole new individual. This is why sexual reproduction produces variation: the offspring's instructions are a fresh mixture, never seen in exactly that combination before.

Once fertilisation has happened, the flower's work as a flower is over, and a great change begins. The petals, having done their job of attracting insects, wither and fall away. Something new starts to form in their place.
concepts.example: 📌 Remember Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. Fertilisation is the joining of the male and female sex cells inside the ovule. Pollination always comes first; fertilisation follows. They are not the same thing.

concepts.title: Seeds and Fruits Form
concepts.explanation:
After fertilisation, the parts of the flower change in a wonderful, orderly way. Follow this carefully, because it explains where every fruit and seed you have ever eaten comes from.

Each fertilised ovule grows into a seed. Inside every seed there are three important things: a tiny baby plant called the embryo, which has the beginnings of a root and a shoot; a food store to feed the embryo until it can make its own food; and a tough protective seed coat wrapped around the outside to keep the embryo safe until conditions are right for growth. A bean, a maize grain, a mango stone, and a date pit are all seeds, each holding a sleeping young plant inside.

At the same time, the ovary — the swollen base of the carpel — grows and ripens into a fruit. The wall of the ovary becomes the flesh of the fruit. So a fruit, in the language of a scientist, is simply a ripened ovary that contains the seeds. This idea often surprises students. A mango is a fruit, and so is a tomato, a bean pod, a papaya, a cucumber, and a chilli — because all of them are ripened ovaries with seeds inside. The sweet flesh of the mango is there to make the fruit attractive to eat, and this, as we will see, is part of the plant's clever plan for spreading its seeds.

Think about a bean plant. Its flower is pollinated, fertilisation happens, and the petals fall. The ovary begins to swell into a long green pod — that pod is the fruit. Inside the pod, each fertilised ovule swells into a bean — those beans are the seeds. When you shell a pod of fresh beans, you are opening a fruit and taking out its seeds. Once you understand this, you will never look at your food in the same way again: much of what you eat is the reproductive success of a plant.

Where those seeds land matters. A place with its own conditions and its own community of living things is a habitat — the shade under a mango tree, a stretch of riverbank, a patch of thorn scrub. Group the habitats of an area together with the soil, water, air and weather they share and you have an ecosystem. The Earth carries many kinds: coral reef, mangrove, savanna, desert, mountain forest. One ecosystem holds many habitats, and a seed that thrives in one may fail a few metres away.

Dispersal usually carries a seed a short way, but people move plants across the world. A species that arrives somewhere new, without the insects and diseases that kept it in check at home, can spread unchecked. Such an invasive species crowds out native plants for light, water and soil, and the animals that fed on those natives lose their food. Prosopis, the thorny tree planted across the Horn of Africa to hold back the desert, now chokes grazing land and waterholes that people and their livestock depended on.

What we add to an ecosystem travels too. A pesticide sprayed on a crop does not stay on the leaf: it washes into soil and water and is taken up by plants and small creatures. Every animal that eats many of them takes in all the poison they carried, so the amount rises at each step of the food chain, and the hunters at the top — big fish, fish eagles, and the people who eat them — carry the heaviest dose of all. This building up is called bioaccumulation, and it is why a chemical that looks harmless in a single spray can damage an ecosystem years later.
concepts.example: 🌟 Did You Know? A single papaya fruit can hold hundreds of small black seeds, and one healthy papaya tree can produce fruit for years. From one tiny seed you plant beside your home, you may harvest thousands of new seeds — a striking picture of how one plant can give rise to a whole future orchard.

methods.title: Dissecting a Flower
methods.example: To take apart a real flower and find its main parts: the sepals, petals, stamens, and carpel.
steps: Place the flower on the white paper so you can see the parts clearly against the pale background.
Gently pull off the green sepals at the base first. Count them and lay them to one side.
Next, carefully remove the petals one by one. Count them. Notice their colour and whether they have a scent.
Now look at the parts left in the centre. Find the stamens — the stalks with small bags (anthers) at the top. Touch an anther gently with your fingertip; the fine dust that comes off is pollen.
Find the carpel in the very centre. Look for the sticky stigma at the top, the style below it, and the swollen ovary at the base.

methods.title: What Does a Seed Need to Germinate? (A Fair Test)
methods.example: To find out which conditions a seed needs in order to germinate, by testing water, warmth, and air one at a time.
steps: You will set up four jars. Each jar changes only ONE condition, so you can see which condition matters. This is called a fair test: you keep everything the same except the one thing you are testing.
Put a layer of cotton wool or folded cloth in the bottom of each jar, and place five beans on top in each.
Jar A (the control): add a little water to dampen the cotton, and leave it on a warm shelf with air. This jar has water, warmth, and air.
Jar B (no water): add NO water. Leave the beans on dry cotton on the same warm shelf, with air.
Jar C (no air): fill this jar right to the top with water so the beans are completely covered and cannot get air. Keep it on the warm shelf.

methods.title: Growing a New Plant Without Seeds (Asexual Reproduction)
methods.example: To grow a whole new plant from just a part of a parent plant, showing asexual reproduction with your own eyes.
steps: Choose your plant part. If using a stem cutting, ask an adult to cut a piece about a hand-span long, just below a point where a leaf grows.
For a stem cutting: stand it in a jar with the cut end in a little water, or push it into moist soil in a pot.
For a sprouting potato: plant it in moist soil with the sprouting 'eye' pointing up.
For an onion or garlic: rest it on the top of a jar so the base just touches water, or plant it shallowly in soil.
Place your plant part on a sunny windowsill. Keep the water topped up or the soil damp.

methods.title: Modelling Seed Dispersal
methods.example: To model how seeds are dispersed by wind, and to see why light, winged seeds travel farther than heavy ones.
steps: Cut two or three small paper 'wings' — for example, thin strips or a simple two-bladed paper spinner — to model wind-dispersed seeds.
Stand in one spot. From the same height each time, drop each object in front of a fan or a breeze: a bean, a stone, and a paper 'winged seed'.
Measure how far from your feet each object lands.
Repeat each drop three times and record the distances so your test is fair.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 1
workedExamples.prompt: Asexual reproduction in plants produces offspring that are: (a) always different from the parent (b) identical to the parent (c) a mix of two parents (d) always larger than the parent
workedExamples.solution: (b) identical to the parent. Asexual reproduction uses one parent and no joining of sex cells, so offspring are clones.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: The male part of a flower is the: (a) carpel (b) stigma (c) stamen (d) sepal
workedExamples.solution: (c) stamen. The stamen (anther and filament) is the male part; remember 'stamen = man'.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: The part of the carpel that catches pollen is the: (a) ovary (b) style (c) filament (d) stigma
workedExamples.solution: (d) stigma. The sticky stigma at the top of the carpel catches pollen grains.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: Pollination is best described as: (a) the joining of sex cells (b) the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma (c) the growth of a seed (d) the ripening of a fruit
workedExamples.solution: (b) the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. This is the definition of pollination; fertilisation comes later.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these is a feature of a wind-pollinated flower? (a) large bright petals (b) sweet nectar (c) feathery stigmas hanging outside (d) sticky pollen held inside
workedExamples.solution: (c) feathery stigmas hanging outside. Wind-pollinated flowers have feathery stigmas outside the flower to catch drifting pollen; the other options describe insect-pollinated flowers.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: Fertilisation happens when: (a) a bee lands on a flower (b) the male sex cell joins the egg cell in the ovule (c) the petals fall off (d) the seed is dispersed
workedExamples.solution: (b) the male sex cell joins the egg cell in the ovule. That joining is fertilisation.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: After fertilisation, the ovule becomes the: (a) fruit (b) petal (c) seed (d) stamen
workedExamples.solution: (c) seed. Each fertilised ovule grows into a seed.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: After fertilisation, the ovary becomes the: (a) seed (b) fruit (c) root (d) stigma
workedExamples.solution: (b) fruit. The ovary ripens into the fruit that surrounds and protects the seeds.

activities.title: Dissecting a Flower
activities.materials: One large flower, such as a hibiscus, a bean flower, a pumpkin flower, or any big garden flower you can find; A sheet of white paper or a plate; A pair of tweezers or your fingers; A magnifying glass if you have one (not essential); A pencil for drawing
steps: Place the flower on the white paper so you can see the parts clearly against the pale background.
Gently pull off the green sepals at the base first. Count them and lay them to one side.
Next, carefully remove the petals one by one. Count them. Notice their colour and whether they have a scent.
Now look at the parts left in the centre. Find the stamens — the stalks with small bags (anthers) at the top. Touch an anther gently with your fingertip; the fine dust that comes off is pollen.
Find the carpel in the very centre. Look for the sticky stigma at the top, the style below it, and the swollen ovary at the base.

activities.title: What Does a Seed Need to Germinate? (A Fair Test)
activities.materials: About 20 dried beans (or maize grains, or lentils) from the kitchen; Four clean jars or cups; Cotton wool, or a folded cloth or paper towel; Water; A refrigerator (for the cold jar)
steps: You will set up four jars. Each jar changes only ONE condition, so you can see which condition matters. This is called a fair test: you keep everything the same except the one thing you are testing.
Put a layer of cotton wool or folded cloth in the bottom of each jar, and place five beans on top in each.
Jar A (the control): add a little water to dampen the cotton, and leave it on a warm shelf with air. This jar has water, warmth, and air.
Jar B (no water): add NO water. Leave the beans on dry cotton on the same warm shelf, with air.
Jar C (no air): fill this jar right to the top with water so the beans are completely covered and cannot get air. Keep it on the warm shelf.

activities.title: Growing a New Plant Without Seeds (Asexual Reproduction)
activities.materials: One of these: a fresh cassava stem cutting, a sprouting potato, an onion or garlic clove, or a stem cutting from a garden plant such as basil or mint; A cup, jar, or small pot; Water, or moist soil in a pot; A sunny windowsill
steps: Choose your plant part. If using a stem cutting, ask an adult to cut a piece about a hand-span long, just below a point where a leaf grows.
For a stem cutting: stand it in a jar with the cut end in a little water, or push it into moist soil in a pot.
For a sprouting potato: plant it in moist soil with the sprouting 'eye' pointing up.
For an onion or garlic: rest it on the top of a jar so the base just touches water, or plant it shallowly in soil.
Place your plant part on a sunny windowsill. Keep the water topped up or the soil damp.

activities.title: Modelling Seed Dispersal
activities.materials: A few small dried seeds or grains (beans, maize) to act as 'heavy seeds'; Paper and scissors to make 'winged seeds' (small paper spinners or paper strips); A small stone or bead as a very heavy 'seed'; A fan, or an open window on a breezy day, or simply your own breath; A tape measure or a length of string to measure distance
steps: Cut two or three small paper 'wings' — for example, thin strips or a simple two-bladed paper spinner — to model wind-dispersed seeds.
Stand in one spot. From the same height each time, drop each object in front of a fan or a breeze: a bean, a stone, and a paper 'winged seed'.
Measure how far from your feet each object lands.
Repeat each drop three times and record the distances so your test is fair.

activities.title: Observe: Fertilisation — The Sex Cells Join
activities.materials: One large flower, such as a hibiscus, a bean flower, a pumpkin flower, or any big garden flower you can find; A sheet of white paper or a plate; A pair of tweezers or your fingers; A magnifying glass if you have one (not essential); A pencil for drawing
steps: Look for an example of fertilisation — the sex cells join around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Method and Wind.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

activities.title: Sort: Seeds and Fruits Form

steps: Look for an example of seeds and fruits form around your home or outside.
Find examples at home and sort them into groups, then explain your rule.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Method and Wind.

rules.title: Two Ways to Make New Plants
rules.text: Plants make new plants in two very different ways, and a great many plants can use both.

rules.title: Asexual Reproduction in Plants
rules.text: Let us look more closely at the clever ways plants make copies of themselves without seeds.

rules.title: The Flower — An Organ Built for Reproduction
rules.text: A flower may look to us like a pretty decoration, but to the plant it is a serious and important organ: it is the structure built entirely for sexual reproduction.

rules.title: Pollination — Delivering the Pollen
rules.text: For sexual reproduction to happen, the male sex cell inside a pollen grain must reach the female egg cell inside an ovule.

rules.title: Fertilisation — The Sex Cells Join
rules.text: Pollination has delivered a pollen grain onto the stigma.

rules.title: Seeds and Fruits Form
rules.text: After fertilisation, the parts of the flower change in a wonderful, orderly way.

realProblems.prompt: Yusuf grows mango trees near Afgooye. He wants every tree in his new orchard to give the same sweet fruit as his best tree. Should he grow them from seeds or by grafting? Explain your choice.
realProblems.answer: He should use grafting. Grafting is asexual reproduction, so every tree is a clone of the best tree and gives the same sweet fruit. Seeds would give varied fruit because they come from sexual reproduction.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Method, Wind, Animals — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: He should use grafting. Grafting is asexual reproduction, so every tree is a clone of the best tree and gives the same sweet fruit. Seeds would give varied fruit because they come from sexual reproduction.

realProblems.prompt: Halima grows maize in a wide block near the Shabelle River rather than in one thin row. Using what you know about how maize is pollinated, explain why a wide block gives a better harvest.
realProblems.answer: Maize is wind-pollinated. In a wide block, the wind can carry pollen from many plants to many others, so more flowers are pollinated and more grains form on each cob. A single thin row would let much pollen blow away without reaching other plants.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Method, Wind, Animals — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: Maize is wind-pollinated. realProblems.prompt: A farmer plants bean seeds in soil that he keeps flooded with water all the time. The seeds rot and do not grow. Explain, using the conditions for germination, what went wrong.
realProblems.answer: The flooded soil left no oxygen (air) around the seeds. Seeds need oxygen to respire and release energy from their food store, so without air they could not germinate and rotted instead.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Method, Wind, Animals — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: The flooded soil left no oxygen (air) around the seeds. Seeds need oxygen to respire and release energy from their food store, so without air they could not germinate and rotted instead.

realProblems.prompt: During the dry season, seeds lie in the baked soil and nothing grows. After the first heavy rains, the land turns green as many seeds germinate at once. Explain why the rain triggers germination.
realProblems.answer: Seeds need water to germinate. During the dry season there is no water, so the seeds stay dormant. The heavy rain provides the water (and the soil is warm), switching on the reactions inside the seeds, so many germinate together.

realProblems.prompt: A goat eats the pods of an acacia tree and later drops the seeds far away in its droppings. Explain two ways this helps the acacia.
realProblems.answer: Two ways: the seed is carried far from the parent, so the seedling does not compete with the parent tree for water and space; and the seed passes through the goat unharmed and is dropped in droppings that act as natural fertiliser, giving it a good start.

realProblems.prompt: A new plant disease arrives that can kill one grafted mango tree. Explain why it could destroy a whole orchard of grafted trees, but might not destroy a group of trees grown from seed. Use the idea of variation.
realProblems.answer: Grafted trees are all identical clones with the same instructions, so if the disease can kill one, it can kill them all — there is no variation to resist it. Seed-grown trees vary because of sexual reproduction, so some may happen to resist the disease and survive.

selfAssessment: I can explain the difference between asexual and sexual reproduction in plants, and give examples of each.
I can describe several methods of asexual reproduction in plants, including runners, bulbs, tubers, and how farmers use cuttings and grafting.
I can name and label the main parts of an insect-pollinated flower and state the job of each part.
I can explain the difference between the male parts (stamen) and the female parts (carpel) of a flower.
I can describe pollination and distinguish between insect pollination and wind pollination.
I can explain fertilisation in a flowering plant and what happens after it.
I can describe how seeds and fruits form from a fertilised flower.
I can explain why seed dispersal matters and describe the main methods plants use to spread their seeds.
